Defense Mechanisms

where the feeling goes · mature or immatureWhere does the feeling go?

Bottom line
  • Name the defense by where the feeling goes: to a safer target (displacement), onto someone else (projection), into its opposite (reaction formation), into an acceptable activity (sublimation)
  • Mature defenses adapt without impairing social functioning (SASH: sublimation, altruism, suppression, humor); immature ones give short-term relief but often cost long-term interpersonal difficulties
  • Suppression is intentional; repression is involuntary

Defense mechanisms are mostly unconscious ways of adapting that protect self-image (suppression is the intentional exception); immature ones appear in children and in adults under stress

Immature defenses
DefenseWhat happensExample
DisplacementMoves a feeling from its upsetting source to a safer targetYelled at by the principal, a teacher criticizes her husband at home
ProjectionAttributes one's own unacceptable feeling to someone elseA man who wants to cheat accuses his wife of infidelity
Reaction formationTurns an unacceptable feeling or impulse into its oppositeA patient with sexual thoughts enters a monastery
Passive aggressionExpresses hostility indirectly, avoiding open conflictAn employee is repeatedly late to get back at a manager
Acting outExpresses unacceptable feelings through impulsive actionsA child throws tantrums; a child with sick parents misbehaves at school; an adolescent turns to promiscuous sex during the parents' divorce
SplittingSees people or situations as all good or all badAll the nurses are cold, all the doctors warm
RegressionReturns to an earlier developmental pattern of coping
DenialBehaves as if a painful reality does not existPlans a full work schedule despite being warned about chemotherapy fatigue
RationalizationJustifies behavior with logical reasons to avoid a difficult truthAfter being fired, says the job did not matter
IntellectualizationFocuses on facts and logic to avoid distressing feelingsA patient with cancer discusses only survival rates
Isolation of affectSeparates feelings from ideas and eventsDescribes a murder in graphic detail without emotion
RepressionInvoluntarily keeps an idea or feeling out of awarenessDoes not remember counseling during a childhood divorce
IdentificationUnconsciously takes on traits, good or bad, of a more powerful personA resident carries his stethoscope like his favorite attending; a child of an abusive father becomes an abuser
UndoingTries to reverse a situation by adopting a new behaviorAfter a fantasy of sabotaging his wife's car, he has it serviced
Mature defenses (SASH)
DefenseWhat happensExample
SublimationChannels an impulse into a socially acceptable activityA teenager's aggression toward a parent goes into sports
AltruismGains satisfaction from helping others, often at a personal costA crime boss makes a large charitable donation
SuppressionDeliberately sets an unwanted feeling aside to copeChooses not to worry about the big game until it starts
HumorUses jokes to deflect anxiety or discomfort
Commonly confused pairs
PairDecides it
Displacement or projectionDisplacement redirects the feeling to a safer target; projection says the other person has it
Suppression or repressionSuppression is intentional and temporary; repression is involuntary
Sublimation or reaction formationSublimation keeps the wish in an acceptable form; reaction formation flips it to the opposite
Intellectualization or rationalizationIntellectualization retreats into facts; rationalization supplies reasons for an action already taken
Displacement or passive aggressionDisplacement hits a safer target; passive aggression expresses the feeling in a roundabout way instead of directly
Acting out or regressionActing out is impulsive action; regression is coping like a much younger person

Pause point. Find the source of the feeling and where it went; the destination names the defense.

Practice
  1. A nurse is criticized harshly by her supervisor and says nothing in reply That evening she snaps at her teenage son over a small mess in the kitchen She later admits her anger was really at the supervisor → Displacement → Anger at a superior redirected onto a safer target is displacement; passive aggression expresses the feeling in a roundabout way instead of directly, and projection attributes the feeling to someone else
  2. A married man privately attracted to a coworker tells no one about it He repeatedly accuses his wife of flirting with other men She has given no cause for suspicion; he denies any interest in anyone else → Projection → Attributing his own unacceptable attraction to his wife is projection; displacement would redirect a feeling to a safer target, and reaction formation would flip it
  3. A 16-year-old has frequent angry outbursts toward his strict father He joins the wrestling team and pours the anger into training His grades and mood improve, and he now competes at the state level → Sublimation → Channeling aggression into an acceptable activity is sublimation, a mature defense; reaction formation would show the opposite feeling, and acting out is impulsive action
  4. A medical student learns the night before an exam that her grandmother was hospitalized She decides to set the worry aside until the exam is over Afterward she calls her family and talks openly about her fears → Suppression → Deliberately and temporarily setting a feeling aside is suppression, a mature defense; repression is involuntary, and denial treats the reality as absent
  5. A 52-year-old man just diagnosed with lung cancer meets his oncologist He asks only about survival statistics and staging systems When asked how he feels about the news, he cites published response rates instead → Intellectualization → Retreating into facts to avoid distressing feelings is intellectualization; rationalization justifies an action, and denial would reject the diagnosis
Pairs with Cluster B Personality Disorders: splitting in borderline personality disorder.
Transferable rule

Find the source of the feeling and where it went; the destination names the defense.
